chunks: Testing PCBs at large scale. The question: How are PCBs testing at a large scale?
Testing a few boards by hand is simple. Testing thousands a day is a systems problem.
You need test stations fast enough to keep up with the line, a cost that makes sense at that volume, and a way to know the test itself still works.
Results are also logged by serial number, so you can spot trends in defects.
Think of airport security. If a passenger arrives every 20 seconds and each screening takes 45 seconds, one lane creates a growing queue. You open more lanes in parallel.
You also check that the scanners still catch a test item, and you keep records to see which times get busy.
A board test cell is the same: match the pace of arrivals, check the checker, and keep data.
A typical high-volume test cell. Results from every station go to a database, used both for pass/fail decisions and for feedback to the line.
Failed boards go to a repair loop, then re-enter the flow.
Takt time: the target time between finished boards that the line must sustain. Fixture: a custom holder with spring-loaded probes that touches many test pads at once.
Parallel test sites: several test positions working at the same time. False fail: a good board wrongly rejected, often from worn probes.
Golden board: a known-good (or known-faulty) board used to check the tester.
The line finishes a board every 20 seconds, but one test takes 45 seconds. One station would fall behind. You need at least 45 / 20 = 2. 25, so 3 stations in parallel.
Next, compare costs. A fixture costs 9,000 USD, then about 0. 50 USD of test time per board.
A flying probe, a few moving probes with no fixture, costs about 800 USD to program but about 5. 33 USD per board, because it is slow. The fixture saves 4.
83 USD per board, so its extra 8,200 USD pays back after 8,200 / 4. 83, about 1,700 boards. That is the whole idea.
"At scale, test is a throughput and cost problem.
I'd use fixtured in-circuit and fast functional test with automatic handling, test several boards or a panel in parallel, and size the number of stations from test time versus line takt.
Fixtures cost thousands but run in seconds, so above some volume, around a couple of thousand boards in a typical example, they beat flying probe.
Every board is serialised and logged, results feed statistical process control, and the testers are calibrated and checked with known-good and known-bad boards.
Designing in test points makes it all possible."
